title: LeakCanary 源码与泄漏引用链检测
key_conclusions: LeakCanary's core path is watch weak reference, wait for GC, dump HPROF, then let Shark compute the shortest strong path from GC Roots to the retained object.
LeakCanary proves Java reachability and ownership paths; it does not by itself prove file descriptor, CursorWindow, socket, or native buffer release.
Leak traces should be decoded as Root, Owner, Bridge, and Victim before choosing a fix.
Resource-wrapper fixes require combined acceptance evidence: LeakCanary retained object gone plus fd, meminfo, StrictMode, or CloseGuard stability.
shallow_points: The article still uses representative LeakCanary traces rather than a real project HPROF decoded line by line.
It does not validate exact LeakCanary, Shark, and AndroidX watcher class names against a specific dependency version in a checked-out source tree.
It does not include a runnable sample that leaks Activity, Fragment view, listener, Handler, and resource-wrapper paths for before/after LeakCanary reports.
It does not compare LeakCanary's shortest path with MAT Path To GC Roots on the same HPROF.
discovered_connections: Day 20's Java reachability versus fd/native resource-lifetime boundary is the central limit of LeakCanary evidence.
Day 15's Root-owner-bridge-victim model is the most compact way to read LeakCanary leak traces.
Day 16, Day 17, Day 18, and Day 19 leak patterns map naturally to LeakCanary report segments: Activity/Fragment victims, MessageQueue owners, singleton owners, and listener/callback bridges.
Day 22 should connect Android Studio Memory Profiler with LeakCanary and fd/meminfo evidence so users do not over-trust one Java heap tool.
Day 23 and Day 24 can deepen this article by opening the same HPROF in raw HPROF, Android Studio, MAT, and Shark.
